opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So, when we started looking at feature attribution, what struck us was just how many methods there were: LIME, DeepLIFT, layer-wise relevance propagation, Shapley value–based approaches, various gradient methods. Each came with its own motivation and its own story, and practitioners were left wondering which one to trust and why they sometimes gave very different answers on the same model.

What we found, first with SHAP and then more broadly in our work on removal-based explanations, is that a large number of these methods are actually doing the same underlying thing. They simulate removing features and observe how the model's behavior changes. Where they differ is along a few specific dimensions: how you remove features, for example replacing them with a baseline, marginalizing over a distribution, or conditioning on the remaining features; what model behavior you're explaining, such as a single prediction, the loss, or dataset-level performance; and how you summarize the effects of all those removals, for instance with Shapley values, leave-one-out, or fitting a linear surrogate.

Once you see methods that way, a few useful things happen. First, you can compare methods on principled grounds instead of anecdotally. You can say, "these two disagree because one uses a baseline and the other uses the conditional distribution," and that's something you can reason about. Second, it connects explainability to established theory. The summary step links directly to cooperative game theory, and the removal step connects to information theory and to cognitive psychology ideas about how people reason through counterfactuals. That gives us axioms and guarantees, not just heuristics. Third, it shows you the gaps. When you lay out the design space, you can see combinations nobody has tried, and you can build new methods intentionally. Fourth, and practically important, it helps users choose. In biomedical settings, where much of my work is, a clinician or biologist needs to know what question a given attribution actually answers, and the unified view makes that explicit.

So for me, unification is how a field matures. It moves explainable AI from a collection of tools toward a science with shared foundations, which you need if you want these explanations to be reliable enough for high-stakes uses like medicine.

r001.rationale: The response says many methods share the process of simulating feature removal and observing how model behavior changes.

r002.rationale: It explains why methods can disagree and how to compare them, but does not state that unification helps explain why the methods fail.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the motivation for that work really came out of frustration, honestly. If you look at the explainable AI literature over the last several years, there's been this explosion of feature attribution methods. You have LIME, you have SHAP and all its variants, you have gradient-based methods like Integrated Gradients, you have occlusion-based approaches, and so on. Dozens of them. And each one is typically introduced in its own paper, with its own notation, its own set of design choices, and its own claims about why it's the right thing to do.

And what happens in practice is that a practitioner, say a clinician or a biologist we're working with, asks a very reasonable question: which method should I use? And the honest answer, until recently, was that we didn't have a principled way to say. People would pick a method because it was popular, or because it was the one implemented in their favorite library, not because they understood how it related to the alternatives.

So the thing we wanted to do was step back and ask: are these methods really that different, or are they actually variations on a small number of underlying choices? And what we found is that a huge fraction of them can be described within a single framework. Essentially, every method has to answer two questions. First, how do you remove a feature from the model? Because you can't just delete an input to a neural network, you have to decide whether you replace it with zeros, or sample from a conditional distribution, or marginalize it out, or retrain the model without it. And second, once you can remove features, how do you summarize the effect of removal into a score? Do you look at removing just one feature, or removing all the others, or do you average over subsets the way Shapley values do?

Once you see it that way, methods that looked totally unrelated turn out to be siblings. They differ in one axis and agree on the other. And that's incredibly useful for a few reasons.

One is that it makes the trade-offs explicit. If two methods disagree on an explanation, now you can point to exactly which design choice is responsible, rather than just saying one is "better." The feature removal choice in particular turns out to matter a lot, and it connects directly to questions about whether you're explaining the model or explaining the underlying data-generating process, which are really different goals.

Another is that it lets you transfer theoretical results. If you prove something about one method, say some robustness property, you often get it for free for its relatives in the framework.

And the third, which I think is the most important for moving the field forward, is that it stops us from reinventing the wheel. When the framework is clear, a new method either fills an empty cell, and then you know what's genuinely new about it, or it doesn't, and you've saved everyone some time. It shifts the conversation from "here's another method" to "here's the right choice for this problem." That's the kind of maturity explainable AI needs if it's going to be trusted in domains like medicine, where the stakes are real.

r001.rationale: It says many methods share a framework based on how features or subsets are removed and how the effects of removal are scored.

r002.rationale: It says the framework clarifies trade-offs and disagreements, but does not state that it helps explain why attribution methods fail.

astra-6.text:
I think a unifying understanding is useful because, when we have many different feature attribution methods, we need to understand what makes them different—and what they have in common. What question is each method actually answering? What assumptions does it make? If two methods give different explanations for the same prediction, we need a principled way to understand why.

A unified framework lets us compare those methods and reason about their properties, rather than treating each one as a separate technique. It can also reveal connections that help us develop better methods.

Ultimately, that matters for the people using these explanations. Assigning an importance score to a feature is not enough; we need to understand what that score means and whether it answers the question the user cares about. That gives us a stronger foundation for making explainable AI useful and trustworthy.

r001.rationale: It discusses comparing methods and their assumptions, but does not identify removing features or feature subsets as a shared principle.

r002.rationale: It says a framework can explain differences between methods, but does not state that it helps explain why methods fail.

sol-6.1.text:
A lot of feature attribution methods seem very different, but they’re trying to answer a similar question: how much did each input feature contribute to a model’s prediction? A unifying understanding helps us identify what these methods share and, more importantly, where their assumptions differ.

For example, what does it mean for a feature to be missing? What are we comparing the prediction against? And how do we distribute credit when features interact? Different choices can produce different explanations, even for the same model and prediction.

Having a common framework lets us reason about those differences, rather than simply choosing whichever explanation looks most intuitive. It also helps us identify desirable properties, understand limitations, and develop better methods. Ultimately, that gives us a stronger foundation for deciding when an explanation is useful and what we can actually conclude from it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions feature contribution and asks what it means for a feature to be missing, but does not identify removing features or feature subsets to assess importance as a shared principle.

r002.rationale: The response says a common framework helps reason about differences and understand limitations, but does not state that it helps explain why attribution methods fail.
